title: Which car has the smallest carbon footprint as the energy system changes?
citation: Šimaitis, J., Lupton, R., Vagg, C., Butnar, I., Sacchi, R. & Allen, S. (2025). Communications Earth & Environment 6, 476.
takeaways: A car's footprint depends on when its energy is made, so the use phase should be time-adjusted.
Electricity decarbonises fastest in every scenario, so BEVs came out 32–47% below hybrids.
FCEVs won only in the 1.5 °C scenario, thanks to carbon-negative BECCS hydrogen.

review.q: Why does a typical LCA overstate a BEV's footprint?
review.a: It uses today's grid for all 10–20 years of driving, though the grid gets cleaner.
The lifetime distance at which a BEV's whole-life footprint drops below a hybrid's.

title: If battery metals get expensive, do fewer people buy electric cars?
citation: Wang, H., Feng, K., Wang, P., Yang, Y., Sun, L., Yang, F., Chen, W.-Q., Zhang, Y. & Li, J. (2023). Nature Communications 14, 1246.
takeaways: In GCAM, metal prices reach EV uptake through battery cost, then cost per passenger-km, then the logit share.
A High price surge cut China's EV share from 49% to 35% (2030) and from 67% to 51% (2060), raising 2020–2060 road CO2 by 28%.
Cobalt-free chemistries (LFP, LMO) and recycling soften the blow; passenger cars are hit hardest.

review.q: Why can a 7–10% rise in EV cost cut the EV share by about 14 points in GCAM?
review.a: The logit with a large exponent turns small cost gaps into big share shifts, especially when options are close in cost.

review.q: Why did LFP batteries soften the impact of the metal price surge?
review.a: LFP contains no cobalt or nickel, so only the lithium price rise reaches the battery cost.

title: Will hydrogen fuel trucks and ships, or mostly factories?
citation: O’Rourke, P., Mignone, B. K., Kyle, P., Chapman, B. R., Fuhrman, J., Wolfram, P. & McJeon, H. (2023). Environmental Science & Technology 57(48), 19508–19518.
takeaways: In below-2 °C runs, hydrogen reached 10–22 EJ in 2050 (2–4% of final energy), and industry used more than transport in most cases.
Cheaper end-use technology (e.g. fuel-cell trucks) raised hydrogen use by 70–84%; adding pipelines and trucks added under 2 EJ and mainly shifted production from on-site to central plants.
Green on-site electrolysis was the largest source (36–69%); a 1.5 °C goal more than doubled hydrogen use to 30–48 EJ.

review.q: In O’Rourke et al. (2023), what mattered more for how much hydrogen gets used: delivery options or end-use costs?
review.a: End-use technology costs. Delivery options mainly changed where hydrogen was made (on site vs central plants).

review.q: Why was most green hydrogen made on site in GCAM’s results?
review.a: On-site electrolysis skips the cost of trucking or piping hydrogen, which is large per unit; over 90% of green hydrogen was on site.
